title: Medicare Supplement (Medigap) Plans
summary: Explains AARP Medicare Supplement Insurance Plans from UnitedHealthcare, including what they cover, plan letters A through N, costs, and when and how to apply.

atoms.title: What a Medicare Supplement plan is
atoms.question: What is a Medicare Supplement plan?
atoms.text: Original Medicare (Part A and Part B) doesn't pay the full cost of covered health care services and supplies. Medicare Supplement insurance (Medigap) plans help pay some of the remaining costs such as medical copayments, coinsurance and deductibles. The plans available depend on the state where you live.

atoms.title: How claims flow with Original Medicare and Medigap
atoms.question: How does a Medicare Supplement plan pay claims?
atoms.text: Original Medicare (Part A and Part B) generally pays about 80% of covered expenses, and you are responsible for the rest. When you receive covered care, your provider bills Original Medicare first. After Medicare pays its share, the provider bills the Medicare Supplement plan, which pays some or all of the rest after your Part B deductible is satisfied. The amount depends on the plan type you choose.

atoms.title: What Medicare Supplement plans do not cover
atoms.question: What do Medicare Supplement plans not cover?
atoms.text: In general, Original Medicare and Medicare Supplement plans don't cover long-term care, such as custodial care in a nursing home, or private-duty nursing services. They also do not cover routine vision, dental, hearing or prescription drugs, though some Medicare Supplement plans offer Wellness extras, which are discounts and additional services to help with these costs. Prescription drug coverage can be obtained separately through a standalone Part D plan (PDP).

atoms.title: Benefits of choosing a Medicare Supplement plan
atoms.question: Why choose a Medicare Supplement plan?
atoms.text: With a Medicare Supplement plan you don't need to shop for or renew your plan each year. Benefits include more predictable out-of-pocket costs, the ability to choose any hospital or doctor that accepts Medicare, no prior authorizations or referrals, coverage anywhere in the United States, and a plan that can't be canceled because of your age, health or number of claims, as long as you pay premiums when due and make no material misrepresentation on your application.

atoms.title: AARP Medicare Supplement plans: UnitedHealthcare scale
atoms.question: How large is UnitedHealthcare's Medicare Supplement business?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare describes itself as the largest Medicare Supplement insurer nationwide, with more than 4 million insured members and 94% of members renewing their plan each year. Plans carrying the AARP name are endorsed by AARP, and some include Wellness extras like dental, hearing and vision discounts plus gym memberships.

atoms.title: Medigap plan letters are standardized by state
atoms.question: Are Medicare Supplement plans the same across insurers?
atoms.text: All Medicare Supplement plans are offered by private insurance companies and regulated by federal and state governments. In most states plans are named with letters, such as Plan A and Plan B, and plans with the same name have the same coverage no matter which company you choose. Not all plans are available in all states. In some states you may also choose a Medicare Select or high-deductible plan, and Massachusetts, Minnesota and Wisconsin have their own standardized plans.

atoms.title: Plan A, B and G benefits compared
atoms.question: How do Medicare Supplement Plans A, B and G compare?
atoms.text: Plan A is the basic benefits plan: Part A inpatient hospital deductible $1,736, annual Part B deductible $283, Part B excess charges not covered. Plan B adds coverage of the Part A deductible ($0). Plan G is the comprehensive plan: Part A deductible $0, Part B deductible $283, Part B excess charges covered, and foreign travel emergency covered at 20% after a $250 annual deductible with a $50,000 lifetime maximum. All three list $0 for primary care, specialist, urgent care and emergency visits.

atoms.title: Plan K, L and N cost-sharing plans
atoms.question: How do Medicare Supplement Plans K, L and N work?
atoms.text: Plan K is the lower premium 50% benefits plan, covering 50% of the Part A inpatient hospital deductible (listed as $868) with 10% coinsurance for primary care, specialist, urgent care and emergency visits. Plan L is the lower premium 75% benefits plan, covering 25% of the Part A deductible ($434) with 5% coinsurance. Plan N is the copay plan, with up to a $20 copay for primary care and specialist visits and up to a $50 emergency care copay; its Part A deductible is $0 and it does not cover Part B excess charges.

atoms.title: Plans C and F are limited to older enrollees
atoms.question: Can I still buy Medicare Supplement Plan C or Plan F?
atoms.text: Plan C and Plan F are only available to those first eligible for Medicare before 2020. Medicare Supplement plans sold to people new to Medicare on or after January 1, 2020, don't cover the Part B deductible. Plan G provides the same benefits as Plan C and Plan F, except for Part B deductible coverage. Plan C and Plan F list a $0 Part B deductible, and Plan F also covers Part B excess charges.

atoms.title: Medigap costs: premium, deductible, copay
atoms.question: What costs come with a Medicare Supplement plan?
atoms.text: Medicare Supplement plan costs can include a monthly premium, which varies by insurance company and can change yearly; a deductible, with Medicare deductible amounts set by the federal government; and a copayment or coinsurance on some plans, though many do not have one. Original Medicare doesn't have an out-of-pocket maximum, while Medicare Supplement plans have predictable costs that help you stay ahead of unexpected out-of-pocket expenses.

atoms.title: When to apply for a Medicare Supplement plan
atoms.question: When can I apply for a Medicare Supplement plan?
atoms.text: The best time to buy a Medicare Supplement plan is during your six-month Medigap Open Enrollment Period (OEP), which starts the first day of the month in which you are age 65 or older and enrolled in Part B. During this time you are guaranteed acceptance, meaning you have a right to buy any Medicare Supplement plan sold in your state. Your plan starts on the first day of the month after your application is approved and your first payment is received, or on a later month you select.

atoms.title: How to apply for a Medicare Supplement plan
atoms.question: How do I apply for a Medicare Supplement plan?
atoms.text: You can apply for a plan online, by phone at 1-833-591-5020 / TTY 711 or with an agent. You'll need: 1) information from your Medicare card, if you have one; 2) other insurance provider information, if applicable, such as current employer insurance, Medicaid or other Medicare Supplement coverage; and 3) your AARP membership number. You must be an AARP member to enroll in an AARP Medicare Supplement Insurance plan.
